gap: No lens looked for indirect prompt injection or agent tool-authorization. The three lenses were hostile input / crypto-identity / correctness; none asked "what happens when untrusted relay text becomes an LLM prompt that drives tool calls." This is the platform's defining feature and its trust boundary was never modelled. Concretely: crates/buzz-acp/src/config.rs:435-444 declares `permission_mode` with `default_value = "bypass-permissions"` and the doc comment "Defaults to bypassPermissions which skips the per-tool-call permission flow"; crates/buzz-acp/src/lib.rs:250 shows `RespondTo::Anyone` is a supported production mode (author_allowed at lib.rs:235-260), so arbitrary relay users' message text can reach the agent prompt while per-tool approval is off. The tools on the other end are crates/buzz-dev-mcp/src/shell.rs (audited in isolation as a sandbox, never as an injection sink) and the MCP servers spawned via crates/buzz-agent/src/mcp.rs.
why_it_matters: The whole audit treats agents as a subprocess-lifecycle problem, not an authorization problem. A channel member posting crafted text to an agent running with --respond-to anyone and the default bypassPermissions is the most plausible full-compromise path in this codebase, and zero findings even address the category.
concrete_followup: Run a fourth lens ("agent trust boundary") over the path: crates/buzz-acp/src/lib.rs (author gate + event->prompt), pool.rs (session/new, apply_permission_mode at pool.rs:999-1107), queue.rs (turn scheduling), crates/buzz-agent/src/llm.rs (request building, 6556 lines, never opened), agent.rs (tool dispatch loop, 1048 lines, never opened), mcp.rs env passthrough, and crates/buzz-dev-mcp/src/shell.rs as the sink. Specifically answer: can a non-owner author's text reach a tool call, and does anything re-check owner identity between prompt and tool execution?

gap: Mobile secrets at rest were never assessed, in either the code or the policy. `mobile/lib/shared/community/community_storage.dart:22` constructs `const FlutterSecureStorage()` with no IOSOptions and no AndroidOptions (flutter_secure_storage ^10.0.0, pubspec.yaml:20), and that store holds the nsec — the file's own migration constants include `_legacyNsec = 'buzz_nsec'` and Community.create() takes `nsec:`. All three mobile passes list community_storage.dart as read in depth, but the at-rest question was never asked, because the crypto lens was scoped to NIP-44/ECDH/pairing. SECURITY.md compounds this: it has a detailed "Desktop Secret Storage — OS Keyring" section covering macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager and the Linux Secret Service, and says nothing whatsoever about the mobile client.
why_it_matters: Without an explicit iOS accessibility class the key inherits the default rather than a `ThisDeviceOnly` class, which governs whether the user's private key leaves the device in an iCloud/iTunes backup; without explicit AndroidOptions the backing store choice is left to defaults. The audit read the file three times and could not see this because no lens covered platform key-storage configuration, and no policy document told it the property mattered.
concrete_followup: Read mobile/lib/shared/community/community_storage.dart with mobile/ios/Runner/Info.plist and android/app/build.gradle.kts, determine the effective keychain accessibility class and Android backing store for flutter_secure_storage 10.x defaults, and check whether the app opts out of Android auto-backup. Then add a Mobile Secret Storage section to SECURITY.md stating the intended guarantee, so the next audit has something to test against.

gap: Client-side binary parsers outside Rust got roughly zero attention, while their Rust twin got four passes. crates/buzz-media/validation.rs was read in full by one breadth and three deep passes (including reading the third-party image/gif/png/mp4 decoder sources), and produced the HIGH GIF logical-screen-vs-frame bomb. The same job on the client side was never done: mobile/lib/shared/relay/animated_image_sanitizer.dart (a hand-rolled PNG/APNG chunk walker, WebP chunk filter and GIF scrubber that runs before upload), mp4_fast_start.dart, and the native sanitizers mobile/android/.../AndroidMediaSanitizer.kt (160 lines) and mobile/ios/Runner/MediaSanitizer.swift (199) plus NativeAttachmentPopover.swift (1,089) were listed as "never opened" by every mobile pass. The project treats these as security-relevant — it ships mobile/test/shared/relay/animated_image_sanitizer_test.dart, mp4_fast_start_test.dart, AndroidMediaSanitizerTest.kt and AndroidImageProcessorTest.kt against them.
why_it_matters: 3,579 lines of Kotlin/Swift are the app's only code with direct OS media, camera and photo-picker access, and not one line was read by any auditor in any phase. The Dart sanitizer parses attacker-influenceable byte streams with manual offset arithmetic (`payloadLength + 12`, `bytes.sublist(typeStart, typeStart + 4)`) — the exact shape that produced the confirmed Rust finding. The asymmetry is purely an artifact of tooling: Rust had clippy and a mature reviewer prior; Dart/Kotlin/Swift had neither.
concrete_followup: Run the hostile-input lens over mobile/lib/shared/relay/animated_image_sanitizer.dart and mp4_fast_start.dart with the same bounds-and-differential method used on validation.rs, then read AndroidMediaSanitizer.kt, MediaSanitizer.swift and NativeAttachmentPopover.swift in full. Specifically check whether the Dart PNG/WebP chunk allowlists and the relay's validation.rs allowlists agree — a divergence is a client-server parser differential of the same family as the two confirmed kind:40003 e-tag findings.

gap: Whole languages and file types got no mechanical ground truth, so those conclusions rest on model reading alone. Dart (50,766 lines in mobile/lib): semgrep's Dart rule coverage is zero by the audit's own admission, and the audit never ran `flutter analyze` even though CI does (ci.yml:857) and mobile/analysis_options.yaml configures flutter_lints plus a `custom_lint` plugin whose project-specific rules nobody enumerated; the 39 pubspec dependencies were never advisory-scanned. Kotlin/Swift (3,579 lines): no linter, no scanner, no reader. Shell (5,689 lines across scripts/, script/, bin/, deploy/): no shellcheck run, and the supply-chain pass only spot-read the release-gating scripts. SQL: all 26 files in migrations/ were skipped as individual files by every db pass — read only through migration.rs's embedded assertions, except 0001, 0006, 0010, 0021 and 0025. The 935-line Justfile was skimmed only.
why_it_matters: For roughly a third of the codebase the audit's output is one model's reading with no independent signal to catch what it missed. The Rust findings were backed by clippy and cargo audit; the Dart findings — including the HIGH mobile kind:40003 edit-forgery — have no such backstop. Migrations are where tenant-isolation constraints and unique indexes actually live, and they were inferred from a Rust file that quotes them rather than read.
concrete_followup: Run `cd mobile && flutter analyze` and record what the audit's manual pass missed; run `dart pub outdated` / an OSV scan on the 39 mobile deps; run shellcheck across scripts/, script/, bin/ and deploy/; and read all 26 migrations/*.sql directly, checking every table for a community_id column plus the unique indexes the db pass assumed exist. Also enumerate the custom_lint rules the project defines — they are project-declared invariants the audit never saw.

gap: The git-on-object-storage subsystem is ~10,000 lines with a 871-line spec, and both were left almost untouched. crates/buzz-relay/src/api/git/ totals 9,858 lines; across all relay passes only mod.rs, hook.rs, policy.rs (partial) and transport.rs (partial) were read — cas_publish.rs, hydrate.rs, store.rs, pack_cache.rs, manifest.rs, manifest_event.rs and binding.rs were explicitly never opened. docs/nips/NIP-GS.md's Security Considerations names concrete threats nobody checked, most sharply: "Repository-local `.gitconfig` can override `gpg.x509.program`. Users SHOULD be aware that cloning an untrusted repository could redirect signing to a malicious program." docs/spec/GitOnObjectStore.tla (271 lines) was never opened either.
why_it_matters: This is remote-code-execution-adjacent surface: git config injection from a cloned repo redirects the signing program, which holds the nsec. The relay side is hardened (transport.rs:309 sets GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM and GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null, and pins core.hooksPath at 1083-1085), and desktop project_git_exec.rs:132-162 does the same plus core.fsmonitor and protocol.file.allow — but only for commands routed through those two files, and neither the desktop project_git family's other 3,480 lines nor buzz-dev-mcp/src/shim.rs:304 (which injects `gpg.x509.program = git-sign-nostr` by unqualified name, not absolute path, contrary to the NIP's own guidance) was audited for bypasses.
concrete_followup: Verify every git subprocess spawn in desktop/src-tauri/src/commands/project_git*.rs, project_terminal.rs and crates/buzz-dev-mcp/src/shim.rs routes through the hardened env builder, and check whether shim.rs:304's PATH-resolved `git-sign-nostr` can be shadowed. Then a first read of api/git/{cas_publish,hydrate,store,pack_cache,manifest}.rs against NIP-GS's Security Considerations and GitOnObjectStore.tla.

gap: Four slices returned findings out of all proportion to their size, and none of them received a deep-dive lens. desktop-rest: 604 files, 30 read, 1 finding. desktop-agents: 322 files, 24 read, 2 findings. tauri-core: 183 files, 14 read, 3 findings — and its own note concedes managed_agents/, huddle/ (10,573 lines), mesh_llm/ (5,993), migration/, archive/, event_sync*.rs and app_state.rs were all skipped. gateway-mesh: 23 files, 1 finding, covering buzz-push-gateway (4,092 lines of Apple App Attest, APNs, grant and authority logic) with config.rs, postgres.rs and metrics.rs skipped and no deep pass ever scheduled. agent-surface likewise got only a breadth pass across four crates totalling 30,738 lines.
why_it_matters: The 3-lens depth phase went to 9 slices chosen up front as risky; the other 8 got one pass each at coverage depth. A low finding count from a one-pass sweep of 604 files is a statement about the sweep, not about the code — and the depth phase reliably multiplied yield elsewhere (tauri-commands went from 4 findings on 5 files to 24 across three lenses). The push gateway in particular mints device-push authority and was never re-examined.
concrete_followup: Schedule depth passes for the four slices, prioritising by unexamined-lines-per-finding: tauri-core's managed_agents/ and huddle/ first (covered above), then buzz-push-gateway end to end (app_attest.rs, grant.rs, authority.rs, postgres.rs, config.rs), then desktop-agents' workflow step/trace rendering and the agentSessionTranscript pipeline that its own note flagged as follow-up.

gap: Fifteen NIP specs carry "Security Considerations" sections that were never diffed against the implementation — and the one time this method was applied it produced three confirmed findings. docs/nips/ holds NIP-AA (Agent Authentication), AE, AM (Agent Turn Metrics), AO (Agent Observability), AP (Agent Personas), CW (Channel Window), DV, ER (Event Reminders), GS, IA, MP (Multi-Repository Projects, shipping its own NIP-MP.fixtures.json and NIP-MP.fold-fixtures.json conformance fixtures), OA, PL (Push Leases, 442 lines), RS (Cross-Device Read State Sync, 796 lines) and WP — roughly 4,300 lines of normative text. Only NIP-OA and NIP-AB were meaningfully cross-checked. NIP-OA alone yielded the three confirmed findings about `conditions` clauses being syntax-checked but never evaluated, each of which was found precisely by reading the spec sentence ("Verifiers MUST evaluate every clause") and then the code.
why_it_matters: These documents are the project's own written contract for what each event kind must and must not permit, and reading them against the code has a demonstrated hit rate in this very audit. NIP-PL (push leases) and NIP-RS (cross-device read state) are the two largest unchecked specs and both govern data that crosses device and tenant boundaries; the NIP-MP fixture files are machine-checkable and were never executed.
concrete_followup: For each of NIP-PL, NIP-RS, NIP-IA, NIP-AA and NIP-AO, extract every MUST/MUST NOT from its Security Considerations section into a checklist and grep for the enforcing code, exactly as was done for NIP-OA. Start with NIP-PL against crates/buzz-relay/src/handlers/push_lease.rs and crates/buzz-db/src/push.rs, and run the NIP-MP fixtures.

gap: Secret leakage through logs, telemetry and the audit chain was never checked, and the one crate that would prove SECURITY.md's tamper-evidence claim was read only in part. crates/buzz-relay/src/telemetry.rs (580 lines) and metrics.rs (207) were listed as never opened by every relay pass; grep finds no redact/skip_serializing/SecretString/zeroize helper in either. crates/buzz-audit (1,114 lines) had only hash.rs and service.rs read, by the tooling-identity breadth pass, which produced no findings — so SECURITY.md's claim that the audit log is a SHA-256 chain "designed for SOX-grade compliance and eDiscovery" is untested. The media slice flagged the same class and could not close it: it noted it "did not review buzz-relay's HTTP handlers that call into this crate to confirm MediaConfig's Debug output is never logged there." The core auditor could only clear buzz-core because that crate has no logging dependency at all.
why_it_matters: Nostr secret keys, NIP-98 auth headers, NIP-44 conversation keys and S3 credentials all pass through structs that derive Debug, and a single `tracing::debug!("{:?}", cfg)` in an unread file writes them to operator logs and any log shipper. This is a whole vulnerability class — credential disclosure via observability — that no lens named. The audit chain is the project's stated compliance control and nobody verified the chaining or the ordering it depends on.
concrete_followup: Grep every crate for `{:?}` / `#[derive(Debug)]` on types carrying SecretKey, nsec, conversation keys, bearer tokens or S3 credentials, and check each logging call site; read crates/buzz-relay/src/telemetry.rs and metrics.rs specifically for what event fields reach spans. Separately read all of crates/buzz-audit (entry.rs, action.rs, hash.rs, service.rs) and confirm the chain link covers the fields SECURITY.md claims, including whether a concurrent writer can interleave and break ordering.
